title: When the Market Moves but the Model Does Not: Stale Financial Information in LLMs
abstract: We study how stale and inaccurate information affect financial forecasts generated by large language models (LLMs), and whether forecast deterioration translates into economically meaningful decisions. Using GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Llama 3.3 70B, we construct matched forecasts for Bitcoin, gold, silver, and the S&P 500 around modelspecific information boundaries. Models forecast under memory-only, verified-information, false-price, and stale-fresh conflict conditions. Memory-based forecasts perform well when the target remains within the model's historical information range, but forecast error rises sharply once the target moves beyond that boundary. Supplying a single verified current observation largely restores forecast accuracy, while a deliberately distorted current price is transmitted strongly into the forecast. When stale and current information are presented together, models place substantially greater weight on the current observation. These effects carry over to investment decisions under a common trading rule: after the information boundary, stale forecasts generate persistent directional exposure and adverse payoffs, whereas verified information materially improves outcomes. The economic magnitude, however, depends on prevailing market conditions, with the estimated effect attenuating after removing common market drift. The results indicate that the reliability of LLM-based financial systems depends not only on model characteristics, but also on the timeliness, accuracy, and ordering of the information supplied to them.
why: LLM knowledge cutoff limits forecasting; tests four major models

title: The Anonymity Paradox: Identity Disclosure, Online Information Production, and Stock Price Efficiency
abstract: The internet real-name system, a major platform governance intervention aimed at enhancing accountability, may inadvertently reshape information production with significant market consequences. This study examines how a front-end real-name policy—the mandatory display of user IP-location information—influences stock price informativeness. Leveraging China’s 2022 policy enactment as a quasi-natural experiment and a difference-in-differences design with firm-quarter data from 2021 to 2023, we find that the policy significantly decreases stock price informativeness, as reflected in a significant increase in stock price synchronicity. Mechanism tests reveal that the policy suppresses user engagement on social investing platforms, reducing both overall and informative post volumes and thereby diminishing retail trading. Consequently, investors shift their information-seeking activities toward official interactive platforms, and stock prices exhibit a stronger response to unexpected earnings. Further heterogeneity analyses show that the increase in stock price synchronicity is larger among firms with weaker governance, lower information disclosure quality, and evasive responses on official investor-interaction platforms, but smaller among firms with higher observed AI-assisted communication usage. These findings suggest that firms’ pre-existing information environments and observed communication practices shape the capital-market consequences of the real-name system. We provide the first evidence on the capital-market effects of front-end real-name disclosure, highlighting a trade-off between regulatory goals and market efficiency and offering insights into the role of firms’ information communication practices in online platform governance.
why: Causal: anonymity reduction suppressed market information production

title: Planning External-Data Adoption in Energy-Market Forecasting: A Matched Decision Framework for Global News
abstract: Energy planners must decide whether to acquire and maintain external data before knowing whether the added information will improve operational forecasts. This paper develops a matched decision framework that converts the forecast gain from an added feed into a model-specific break-even adoption threshold. The framework closes news windows before each forecast, holds target dates, rows, model selection, and calibration fixed, and then compares market-only (M0) with news-augmented (M1) forecasts. We apply it to nine daily energy-return series from 3 January 2020 to 17 April 2026 using traditional, domain-trained deep, and pretrained time-series models. Adding Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone news raises mean absolute error (MAE) by 0.018 for long short-term memory, 0.026 for a causal Transformer, and 0.018 for a Temporal Fusion Transformer; all three block-bootstrap intervals remain above zero after Holm adjustment. Ridge instead lowers MAE by 0.016, while the random-forest and foundation-model intervals span zero. The planning layer expresses each gain as a percentage of market-only MAE. Ridge supports adoption only when the loss-equivalent feed cost is below a robust threshold of 0.635%; the three deep models retain market-only information even at zero feed cost, and the remaining comparisons support deferral or redesign. Market-only Temporal Fusion Transformer records the lowest MAE among 16 model-information combinations, while calibration effects vary across forecast cells. By separating model selection from data-source adoption, the framework turns retrospective forecast evaluation into a prospective procurement and governance rule for asynchronous external feeds.
why: Negative result: external news worsens forecasts uniformly

title: Forecasting, Forward Contracting, and Retailer Performance in a Regulated Electricity Market
abstract: Forecast improvements are widely expected to enhance trading performance, yet their economic value depends on how forecast information is incorporated into contracting decisions. This paper studies the interaction between spot price forecasting and forward contracting in a regulated, sequential electricity market. We first develop an integrated framework that embeds month-ahead spot price forecasts and retailer portfolio choices into a forward equilibrium model. Then, using data from China's Guangdong wholesale market, we demonstrate that while a hybrid approach combing structural modelling with machine learning substantially improves forecasting accuracy, the improvements alone do not guarantee higher profitability. Economic gains arise only when retailers can flexibly adjust forward positions in response. We further document pronounced heterogeneity across retailers of varying sizes and regulatory conditions. Overall, the results illustrate how the value of information in electricity markets is shaped by forward contracting institutions and regulatory design.
why: Real market execution shows forecast gains need flexibility

title: Are Aliases Neutral? Company-Name Form in LLM Equity Valuation
abstract: LLM valuation experiments conceal firm identity behind invented company names to defuse look-ahead bias and treat the substitute label as neutral. Whether it is neutral remains untested. This study tests it with a preregistered equivalence design. I crossed 60 matched pairs of generated names, differing in model-rated pronunciation ease, with nine fictional company profiles and three commercial models, collecting 27,762 responses under a plan frozen before collection and registered before the confirmatory analysis. Holding operating information fixed, easier names were valued 0.5% higher, about $0.25 on a $50 share. The registered tests establish neither that this gap lies within a 1% tolerance nor that it differs from zero. The labeling policy itself, however, was not inert. Secondary estimates without confirmatory verdicts indicate that every model valued the firms 0.8% to 2.6% lower under generated names than under an unnamed profile. Calling the label arbitrary raised valuations by 0.6% and narrowed the pooled name gap. Asserting that pronounceable names signal quality widened the gap in one-year return guesses by 8.8 percentage points, where the models otherwise almost always answered zero. In these settings, a generated label acts as an experimental input, so the alias policy belongs in the design.
why: Rigorous preregistered test finds company names bias LLM valuations.

title: Data Leakage-Free Explainable AI for Decentralized Credit Scoring: A SHAP-Interpretable Approach to Default Prediction
abstract: The integration of machine learning into decentralized finance (DeFi) credit assessment is frequently undermined by opaque algorithms and severe methodological flaws regarding data leakage. This paper presents a rigorous, fully reproducible framework for explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in invoicebacked default risk modeling. Utilizing a highly imbalanced dataset of 12,000 corporate loan originations, we engineer an XGBoost ensemble model that achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.89. We systematically eliminate the pervasive data leakage associated with the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) by implementing a dynamic cross-validation pipeline, ensuring synthetic data generation is strictly isolated to training folds. To satisfy institutional accounting standards for expected loss (e.g., IFRS 9), we mathematically formulate and validate the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), achieving a highly calibrated probabilistic output of 0.08. Furthermore, we extract local explanations using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), imposing strict constraints on the background reference dataset to guarantee mathematical additivity and prevent stochastic approximation transitions. Our findings reveal that Days Payment Outstanding (DPO) and invoice age are primary default drivers, while on-chain reputation effectively mitigates perceived risk. Finally, we address critical privacy vulnerabilities, mathematically modeling Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) on synthetic records. This work establishes a regulatory-compliant, structurally sound ML foundation for permissionless credit provision.
why: Solid credit risk framework but standard methodology, limited novelty.

title: Artificial Intelligence in International Finance: An Empirical Comparison of Traditional and Machine-Learning Models for EUR/USD Forecasting Author
abstract: This study investigates the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning in international-finance exchange-rate forecasting. The research compares a traditional ARIMA model with Random Forest and multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural-network models for forecasting the monthly EUR/USD exchange rate. The dataset contains 192 monthly observations from January 2010 to December 2025 obtained from the Federal Reserve Board's foreign-exchange series distributed through FRED. The sample is divided chronologically into a training period covering January 2010 to September 2022 and an out-of-sample test period covering October 2022 to December 2025. Machine-learning models use the previous twelve monthly exchange-rate observations as predictors, while ARIMA is selected using AIC from a small grid of candidate specifications. Forecast performance is evaluated using MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and directional accuracy. The results show that the Random Forest model achieved an RMSE of 0.0231 and MAPE of 1.76%, while the MLP achieved an RMSE of 0.0229 and MAPE of 1.75%. These errors were lower than those of the ARIMA benchmark, which produced an RMSE of 0.1156 and MAPE of 9.71%. The findings indicate that nonlinear machine-learning models can provide useful forecasting information for EUR/USD in the examined sample, while also highlighting the importance of out-of-sample validation and the limitations of relying on historical patterns alone.
why: Standard FX forecasting lacking novelty, no discussion of transaction costs.

title: RCSB Protein Data Bank: Tools for Analysis and Visualization of Biological Macromolecules
abstract: Through the RCSB.org research-focused web portal, many millions of users access rigorously validated, expertly biocurated, 3D biostructure information stored in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) archive alongside predicted Computed Structure Models (CSMs) from AlphaFold DB and ModelArchive. Specialized tools and related resources, from 3D visualization to protein annotations, allow deep exploration of this rich trove of data. The recently updated RCSB.org Advanced Search interface provides a more intuitive experience with enhanced support for 3D structure exploration. The 3D Similarity Search option is powered by a new AI-based system that is more accurate and scalable to much larger collections of structures. Additional capabilities are provided through web-based APIs and a Python API wrapper package that enable researchers to easily interact with RCSB PDB programmatic services for individually tailored analyses. These resources, together with a statistics tool, training and documentation, and the upcoming wwPDB ID and archive transition, are described.
why: Off-topic: protein structures unrelated to finance
